title: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing
description: Understand CORS, preflight requests, and cross-origin security.

options.text: CORS restrictions are enforced by the server
options.explanation: CORS is enforced by the BROWSER. The server sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers, but it's the browser that checks them and blocks the response from reaching JavaScript. Server-to-server requests are unaffected by CORS.

options.text: A preflight OPTIONS request is sent for any cross-origin request with custom headers or non-simple methods
options.explanation: Simple requests (GET/POST with standard headers and content types) go directly. Non-simple requests (PUT, DELETE, custom headers, application/json) trigger a preflight OPTIONS request to check if the server allows the actual request.

options.text: Setting Access-Control-Allow-Origin to * allows credentials (cookies) to be sent
options.explanation: Wildcard * and credentials are mutually exclusive. To send cookies cross-origin, the server must specify the exact origin AND set Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. The client must also set fetch({ credentials: 'include' }).

options.text: CORS prevents the server from receiving cross-origin requests
options.explanation: The server ALWAYS receives and processes the request. CORS only prevents the browser from exposing the response to JavaScript. This is a common misconception — CORS is not a security mechanism for the server, it's a browser policy.
